title: Teacher Education & Training Models

pts: Pre-service training prepares new teachers before independent classroom practice; in-service training develops practising teachers' ongoing skill.
These stages demand genuinely different approaches — pre-service training addresses foundational unknowns; in-service training addresses specific, experience-informed gaps.
This series itself spans both — usable as foundational pre-service content and as targeted in-service reference.

v: Teacher education; DIET faculty or teacher educators

items: Divide the group in two. One half lists what a D.El.Ed or B.Ed trainee most needs before their first class; the other lists what a teacher with fifteen years’ experience most needs.
Groups display their lists.
Compare: which needs overlap? Which are unique to each stage?
Discuss how the design of a session should differ for each group.
Ask real trainees and experienced teachers to write the lists themselves, then compare with the educators’ guesses.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Pre-service education addresses foundational unknowns; in-service development addresses specific, experience-informed gaps. This book is designed to serve both: Parts I and II as foundations, Parts III and IV as targeted reference.

body: Purpose: to contrast pre-service and in-service needs. Content: a new teacher at a door labelled ‘first class’ with a backpack of basics, and an experienced teacher at a crossroads with specific signposts. Style: warm, clean. Board version: two lists under two headings.

pts: Craft models emphasise learning through observation and supervised practice with an experienced practitioner.
Applied science models emphasise learning theory and research first, then applying it to practice.
Reflective practitioner models, drawing on Schön (Unit 9, Unit 75), emphasise ongoing reflection on one's own evolving practice.
points.who: Wallace's models of professional education, applied to language teaching

v: Teacher education; trainee or in-service teachers

items: Introduce Wallace’s three models briefly.
Give groups cards describing typical training activities.
Groups sort the cards under craft, applied science or reflective.
Each participant marks which activities formed most of their own training.
Discuss the strengths and limits of each model, and what a balanced programme would include.
Groups analyse the timetable of a real D.El.Ed or B.Ed programme and estimate the proportion of each model.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Watch the mentor teach and copy her lesson structure. (craft)
Attend a lecture on Krashen’s input hypothesis. (applied science)
Teach a lesson, watch a recording of it, and discuss one decision with a peer. (reflective)
T: Which kind dominated your B.Ed?
S1: Lectures, mostly. We practised teaching only in the last months.
T: Then your reflective learning began in school, often alone.

body: Purpose: to summarize Wallace’s models. Content: three panels: an apprentice beside a master (craft), a textbook with an arrow to a classroom (applied science), and a circular arrow linking practice and reflection (reflective). Style: clean, parallel. Board version: three icons with labels.

items: Wordwall (free basic version) group-sort activity.

blocks.x: Activity cards sorted into three piles.

pts: Trainee teachers often struggle to translate theoretical training content into actual classroom practice, echoing Unit 79's cognition-versus-belief gap.
Training models that integrate theory directly with supervised practice tend to close this gap more effectively than purely theoretical courses.
This series' consistent effort to ground theory in concrete practical application reflects this same design principle.

items: Trainees recall an English teacher from their own schooling and list three things that teacher did.
Introduce Lortie’s (1975) apprenticeship of observation: years as pupils shape beliefs about teaching.
Trainees compare their list with one principle from their theory course (for example, meaningful input or learner talk time).
Each trainee identifies one belief from their schooling that conflicts with the principle.
Trainees plan one small classroom move that puts the principle into practice in their next lesson.
Trainees revisit the list after the practicum and note what changed.
Support: provide a list of principles to choose from.
Challenge: trainees explain the conflict using the idea of teacher cognition (Unit 79).

blocks.x: From a trainee’s notes (written for this book):

lines: My teacher read the lesson aloud and explained it in Kannada. We copied answers from the board. I learned in college that learners need to use English themselves.
One move: after reading, ask pairs to answer two questions orally before writing.

blocks.x: Integrating theory with practice, rather than teaching them in separate terms, tends to narrow the gap.

body: Purpose: to show theory and practice connected by small moves. Content: two cliffs labelled ‘theory’ and ‘practice’ with a bridge made of planks, each labelled with a small classroom move. Style: simple, encouraging. Board version: two blocks joined by a series of short lines.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared reflective journal.

blocks.x: A two-column page in the notebook: ‘What I was taught’ and ‘What I will try’.

pts: Supervised practicum experience, with structured feedback, remains one of the most consistently valued components of teacher training.
This connects directly to Unit 68's mentoring principles, applied specifically to initial teacher training rather than ongoing development.
The quality of practicum supervision matters as much as its mere existence.

v: Teacher education; practicum supervisors, mentors and trainees
20 minutes before, one lesson, 20 minutes after

items: Pre-observation: the trainee chooses one focus, for example instructions or pair work, and explains the lesson plan.
Observation: the supervisor records only evidence related to that focus.
Post-observation: the trainee speaks first about what happened.
The supervisor shares evidence, asks questions and suggests one change.
The trainee writes one action point for the next lesson.
Trainees observe each other in pairs using the same cycle (Unit 68).
Support: provide a focus sheet with prompts.
Challenge: trainees choose their own focus and design the observation sheet.

blocks.x: A post-observation conversation (written for this book):

lines: A: How did the pair work go?
B: Noisy. I am not sure they understood the task.
A: I noted that four pairs at the back started in Kannada and then asked their neighbours. What happened just before?
B: I gave the instructions once, very quickly.
A: What could you try next time?
B: Model it with one pair first, then ask a learner to repeat the instructions.

blocks.x: Supervision quality matters as much as its existence: focused, evidence-based feedback is more useful than a general score.

body: Purpose: to show the observation cycle. Content: three connected circles: ‘plan and focus’, ‘observe evidence’, ‘talk and act’, with small figures of trainee and supervisor in each. Style: clean cycle. Board version: three circles with arrows.

items: Google Forms (free) for a digital observation sheet; a phone camera for recording, with consent.

blocks.x: A paper observation sheet with a single focus.

body: In post-observation talk, let the trainee speak first and keep your own comments to one strength and one change. Trainees who leave with one clear action point are more likely to act on it than those who leave with a long list.

pts: Teacher qualification requirements and pathways vary enormously across countries and institutional contexts.
Understanding this variation matters for teachers considering international career moves or evaluating colleagues' varied backgrounds.
This connects to Unit 71's discussion of institutional constraints — qualification requirements are themselves a form of language-education policy.

v: Teacher education; trainee or in-service teachers

Groups place each on a chart: pre-service or in-service; national or international; what it assesses.
Groups discuss which qualifications suit which career goals.
Each participant identifies one qualification or course that fits their next step.
Invite a colleague with an international qualification to describe the process.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

pts: Research on teacher training effectiveness supports sustained, practice-embedded development over one-off workshop-style training.
This directly reinforces Unit 68's mentoring-culture argument and Unit 67's action-research approach as genuinely evidence-supported development models.
Isolated, short training sessions without follow-up support show consistently weaker impact on actual classroom practice.

v: Teacher education; DIET faculty and resource persons
The agenda of a recent one-day training

items: Groups examine the agenda of a real or typical one-day workshop.
Using the research summary, groups list what the agenda lacks: practice, follow-up, collaboration, coaching.
Groups redesign it as a term-long programme with the same total time.
Groups present the redesign and the evidence behind each change.
Redesign a cascade training so that each level includes practice and follow-up, not only transmission.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Original: One day, six hours, five presentations, a feedback form.

Redesign: Two hours of demonstration and practice; each teacher tries one strategy in class; a cluster meeting after three weeks to share videos or notes; a peer visit; a final meeting to review learners’ work.

blocks.x: Sustained, practice-embedded development tends to show more impact on classroom practice than isolated sessions (Darling-Hammond, Hyler, and Gardner 2017), and connects with action research (Unit 67) and mentoring (Unit 68).

body: Purpose: to contrast one-off and sustained development. Content: on the left, a single large block labelled ‘one day’; on the right, a series of smaller linked blocks across a term: ‘learn’, ‘try’, ‘share’, ‘visit’, ‘review’. Style: clean. Board version: one box beside five small connected boxes.

items: Google Meet (free, with time limits for group calls on free accounts) or WhatsApp (free) for follow-up between meetings.

blocks.x: Cluster meetings at the resource centre with shared notebooks.

body: Bruce Joyce and Beverly Showers (2002) found that teachers who received coaching in the classroom after training were far more likely to use new strategies than those who received training alone. Theory and demonstration build knowledge; practice with feedback and coaching builds use.

pts: Ongoing professional development remains necessary throughout a teaching career, not just during initial qualification.
This connects directly to Unit 72's career-stage development content, and this series' own structure across four escalating tiers.
Sustained, career-long development, not front-loaded initial training alone, is what evidence increasingly supports.

items: Teachers identify their career stage and one area they want to develop (Unit 72).
They choose a mix of activities: reading, observation, action research, online courses, collaboration.
They plan the year, with approximate hours for each activity.
They identify one piece of evidence of change in their classroom.
They share plans in groups and agree to review them at the end of the term.
A school or cluster creates a shared CPD calendar.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

points.h: This Series as a Training Artefact
pts: This hundred-poster series is itself an example of the kind of structured, theory-grounded, practice-connected training model this poster has described.
Its progression from foundational practice through integration, specialisation, and theory mirrors the very training-model literature just surveyed.
This is a deliberate design choice, not a coincidence — good training practice was applied to building this series itself.

dek: Unit 90 of 100: how the practitioners delivering everything in this series are themselves developed — the models, debates, and evidence behind teacher training.

aims.x: Every unit in this book assumes a teacher who can put it into practice. This unit turns to how such teachers are prepared and developed: the stages of teacher education, the models behind them, the gap between theory and practice, the role of the practicum, the landscape of qualifications, and the evidence on what kinds of development change classrooms. It is written especially for teacher educators, DIET faculty and mentors, but every teacher is also a manager of their own development.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish the aims of pre-service and in-service teacher education;
describe craft, applied science and reflective models of professional education;
explain the theory–practice gap and design activities that bridge it;
run a structured observation and feedback cycle in a practicum;
map the main qualification pathways for English teachers in India and internationally;
use research evidence to redesign a one-off workshop as sustained development;
plan career-long professional development for yourself or others.

why: Why this matters. This entire series is itself a form of teacher development. Understanding how such development actually works, and what evidence supports it, closes an important loop.

background.x: Michael Wallace (1991) described three broad models of professional education for language teachers. In the craft model, trainees learn by watching and imitating an experienced practitioner. In the applied science model, they learn theory and research first and then apply it. In the reflective model, which Wallace favoured, received knowledge and experiential knowledge are brought together through cycles of practice and reflection. The reflective model draws on Donald Schön’s (1983) account of how professionals think in action, which Unit 72 examined in depth.

From the late 1990s, Donald Freeman and Karen Johnson (1998) argued that the knowledge base of language teacher education should start from teachers as learners, their contexts and their activity of teaching, not from linguistics and SLA theory alone. Johnson (2009) developed a sociocultural perspective in which teachers learn through mediated participation in real practice, a view that links this unit with Unit 83. Long before this, Dan Lortie (1975) noted that new teachers bring years of ‘apprenticeship of observation’ from their own schooling, which shapes their beliefs strongly (Unit 79).

Research on professional development is broadly consistent: sustained, practice-embedded development with collaboration, coaching and follow-up tends to change classroom practice more than one-off workshops (Joyce and Showers 2002; Darling-Hammond, Hyler, and Gardner 2017), although Mary Kennedy (2016) cautions that the mechanisms matter more than surface features such as duration.

In India, pre-service education includes the D.El.Ed, often delivered through DIETs, and the B.Ed; NEP 2020 proposes a four-year integrated B.Ed as the eventual minimum qualification and recommends that teachers take part in continuing professional development each year (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) [VERIFY paragraphs 5.15 and 15.5]. In-service training has often used cascade models, in which content passes from state to district to cluster, with the risk of dilution at each step. DIETs, block and cluster resource centres, and platforms such as DIKSHA give Karnataka a rich infrastructure; the challenge is to make development sustained, practical and owned by teachers.

items: Needs comparison. A table contrasting pre-service and in-service needs, with design implications.
Observation cycle. A record of one full pre-observation, observation and post-observation cycle with an action point.
Workshop redesign. A term-long redesign of a one-day training, with evidence for each change.
CPD plan. A personal annual development plan with activities, hours and evidence of change.

terms.def: A model of teacher education in which trainees first learn theory and research findings and then apply them in the classroom (Wallace 1991); contrast the craft model and the reflective model.
Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.
A method of in-service teacher training in which content passes down from state to district to cluster levels; its risk is that ideas are diluted at each step.

The ongoing learning teachers undertake throughout their careers, through training, reading, reflection, research and collaboration with colleagues, for example in DIET programmes or teacher networks.
A model of teacher education in which trainees learn by watching and imitating an experienced practitioner (Wallace 1991); contrast the applied science model and the reflective model.
Professional development for practising teachers, such as DIET workshops, school-based mentoring or online courses, as distinct from pre-service teacher education before entering the profession.
A structured sequence for classroom observation: a pre-observation conversation to agree a focus, the observed lesson, and a post-observation conversation to reflect and plan next steps.
The supervised teaching practice component of a teacher education programme, in which trainees teach real classes with guidance and feedback.
Initial teacher education undertaken before a teacher begins employment, such as a D.El.Ed or B.Ed programme, combining coursework in subject and pedagogy with a supervised practicum.

A model of professional education in which received knowledge from research and experiential knowledge from practice are brought together through cycles of practice and reflection (Wallace 1991). It contrasts with the craft and applied science models.
